blocks.content: The Director of CBI has been provided security of tenure in office by the CVC Act, 2003.

items: CBI is neither a statutory nor a constitutional body; it is an executive body created by a government resolution.
State government consent is mandatory for the CBI to extend its jurisdiction to a state, unless mandated by the Supreme Court or High Courts.
The statutory committee for recommending the appointment of the CBI Director was mandated by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The CBI is not a statutory body; it derives its investigative powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946.
The Director of CBI is provided security of tenure with a minimum period of two years under the CVC Act, 2003.
Selection of the CBI Director is made by a committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court Judge.
The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) exercises superintendence over the CBI in matters related to the Prevention of Corruption Act.
General administrative control and superintendence over the agency rest with the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
